                    ### Question
                    A 59-year-old male presents to the emergency room with shortness of breath. Ten days ago, he was in the cardiac critical care unit after receiving a balloon angioplasty and a bare metal stent for an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). On physical examination, a holosystolic murmur is heard at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla. You also detect an S3 and bilateral crackles in the lung bases. What is the most likely etiology of this patient's acute decompensated heart failure?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Rupture of the anterior papillary muscle on the right ventricle
opb. Rupture of the posterior papillary muscle on the right ventricle
opc. Rupture of the septal papillary muscle on the right ventricle
opd. Rupture of the anterolateral papillary muscle of the left ventricle
ope. Rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle of the left ventricle

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient has a history of STEMI, which increases the risk of myocardial damage and subsequent complications such as papillary muscle rupture. The presence of a holosystolic murmur at the apex, along with signs of heart failure (S3 and crackles), suggests mitral regurgitation, commonly due to papillary muscle rupture. The posteromedial papillary muscle of the left ventricle is particularly susceptible to rupture following inferior STEMI, which is often associated with right coronary artery occlusion. This aligns with the consensus that the posteromedial papillary muscle is the most commonly affected in such cases, making it the likely etiology of this patient's acute decompensated heart failure.
